opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, it shook me quite a bit. Before ChatGPT came out, I had a fairly clear picture in my head: do a PhD, publish good papers, go on the academic job market, and become a professor. That path felt like the natural way to do meaningful research and have independence.

But when ChatGPT arrived, it made something very concrete for me — the frontier of AI was moving incredibly fast, and a lot of that movement was happening in industry, in places with huge compute and large, tightly coordinated teams. As a student, you'd look at what a single lab with a handful of PhD students and a modest GPU budget could do, and compare it with what a company could do by scaling up, and the gap felt enormous. Some of the questions I cared about suddenly seemed like they might be answered — or made irrelevant — by scale before I could even finish a paper on them.

So I started asking myself: what is the unique role of a professor now? If the most impactful empirical work requires resources that universities don't have, then maybe the academic path isn't automatically the best way to have impact. That was uncomfortable, because I had been quite attached to that identity.

At the same time, it didn't make me completely give up on academia. I think it forced me to be more precise about why I'd want to be a professor. It's not just "doing research" anymore. It's things like training people, thinking about longer-term or more fundamental questions that companies may not prioritize, studying these systems from the outside with some independence, and having the freedom to pursue directions that aren't tied to a product roadmap. Those things still matter, maybe even more now.

So I'd say ChatGPT changed my feeling from "becoming a professor is the obvious goal" to "becoming a professor is one option, and I need a really good reason for choosing it." It made the decision much more deliberate.

r001.rationale: The response says ChatGPT made Kay question academia’s impact and choose the professor path more deliberately. It does not attribute newfound confidence to ChatGPT helping write funding proposals.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, before ChatGPT came out, becoming a professor was the whole plan. I'd done the PhD, I was doing the postdoc, and the path felt very clear: publish, get a faculty position, build a lab, train students. That was the dream, and it was a dream I'd had for a long time.

Then ChatGPT happened, and the thing I felt wasn't excitement at first. It was closer to anxiety. I remember using it and realizing that a lot of the questions I was working on in my own research had just been, if not solved, at least made to look small. The gap between what one person in a university lab could do with a handful of GPUs and what a company with thousands of them could do suddenly felt enormous. I started asking myself: if I become a professor, what am I actually going to work on? Am I going to spend five years on a problem that an industry lab solves in a quarter because they have ten times the compute and the data?

That was the first shift. The second one was more personal. I think I had been attracted to academia partly for the freedom and partly because it felt like the place where the frontier was. And ChatGPT made it very obvious that the frontier had moved. The most interesting experiments, the ones that would tell you what these models can really do, were happening inside companies, not in papers. So the question became whether I cared more about the title and the lifestyle of being a professor, or about being close to where the actual discovery was happening.

I don't think the answer is that academia is dead. There's still real work to do on understanding these systems, on evaluation, on safety, on the science of why they behave the way they do, and a lot of that doesn't need the biggest model. But I had to be honest with myself that my original picture of professorship, the one where I'd be building the thing itself, probably wasn't realistic anymore. So ChatGPT didn't kill the dream so much as force me to rewrite it. It made me ask what I actually wanted, rather than what I'd assumed I wanted since grad school.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes anxiety and doubts about becoming a professor after ChatGPT, and does not attribute newfound confidence to ChatGPT helping write funding proposals.

astra-6.text: ChatGPT made me rethink what I would want to contribute as a professor. If students can get an explanation instantly, then teaching has to be about more than delivering information. It has to help them ask better questions, evaluate answers, and develop their own judgment. That’s both unsettling and exciting. It makes me less certain about the traditional role, but more interested in what that role could become.
